processing: Details for this lot are not documented. As is typical of Darjeeling whites, the leaf is minimally handled: withered and dried with little or no rolling.
harvest_season: Described as a second-flush tea; Darjeeling's second flush generally falls in early summer.
appearance_dry: As with other fine Darjeeling whites, likely long, lightly twisted leaf with pale silvery tips; the top SFTGFOP1 leaf grade points to a tippy lot.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Darjeeling whites, a pale gold, clear liquor.
appearance_wet: Typical of the style, soft whole buds and leaves in light olive and tan.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists for this lot. Darjeeling whites generally give a light, sweet, softly floral cup with little astringency.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for a delicate white: cooler water and a long steep. Hotter water brings out dryness at the cost of the sweetness.

vintage_note: Sold by flush and year like other estate Darjeelings, and this name is tied to a second-flush SFTGFOP1 grade. Whites of this kind are normally bought in the current year for freshness. Check the year on the lot, because little beyond the name and grade is published.
description:
This is a white tea from Okayti, an estate in the Mirik Valley of Darjeeling, close to the Nepal border. White tea is not what Darjeeling is known for, which makes it a curiosity, and little is documented about this lot beyond the name: an organic second-flush white, graded SFTGFOP1, the top of the Darjeeling leaf scale.

The making follows the logic of the class. As with other whites, the leaf is handled as little as possible, which keeps it close to its natural state. The grade concerns leaf and tips, not flavour, so treat it as a signal of appearance.

Expect what is typical of Darjeeling whites and not a specific profile: a light, sweet cup with soft florals and little grip. Brew with water around 80 C and give it about three minutes.

When shopping, ask for the year and the flush, and be careful with the word imperial, which is a selling name and not a regulated grade. A sensible comparison is another Darjeeling white, or a Chinese Bai Mu Dan to see how the same idea changes with place.
history:
Okayti was planted by British planters in the 1870s under the name Rangdoo, and its factory dates from 1888. The name change followed the estate's market reputation, by the usual account as the only tea buyers called okay. It was run for more than two decades by the Kumbhat family; a later acquisition by Rajeev Baid of the Evergreen Group is reported, though accounts differ on the current owner.

Little is documented on the Imperial white itself, including when it was first made.
